cleanIntro: The Model 60 is a simple blowback .22 self-loader and the whole strip is two screws, an assembly post and a bolt. What makes it worth doing carefully is the recoil spring, which is live and compressed the moment the action leaves the stock, and the order of the bolt removal — the MUZZLE end of the bolt lifts first, never the rear. The tubular magazine is emptied by cycling the action, not by dropping a magazine, and the orange follower showing in the feedthroat is the only positive empty indication the rifle gives. Marlin's own view is that the bore rarely needs cleaning on modern ammunition; what needs cleaning is the action, every 250 rounds or so, because .22 rimfire loads the receiver with wax and carbon. Further disassembly of the action beyond this strip is not recommended by the maker, so there is no Deep Clean branch here.

steps.title: Safety on SAFE, inner tube locked, then cycle it dry
steps.action: Put the safety on SAFE, confirm the inner magazine tube is locked in place, and then cycle the action repeatedly — charging handle all the way back, let it snap forward — until nothing more is ejected. When the last round leaves, the automatic bolt hold-open engages and the bolt stays back. Keep your fingers off the trigger and the muzzle in a safe direction for every stroke.
steps.quote:
Be sure the inner magazine tube is locked
in place. Cycle the action repeatedly by
pulling the charging handle all the way
back and letting it snap forward (See J).
Repeat this action until the ejection of cartridges ceases.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — How to Unload — p.6

steps.title: Look for the orange follower in the feedthroat
steps.action: Now look, and look at the right thing. Check the chamber and the feedthroat visually — when the magazine is genuinely empty the ORANGE magazine follower is visible in the feedthroat. That orange is the only positive empty indication this rifle gives you; the bolt hold-open is a mechanical device and Marlin says plainly that any mechanical device can fail.
steps.quote:
Any mechanical device can fail, so ALWAYS CHECK THE CHAMBER AND
FEEDTHROAT VISUALLY TO BE SURE NO CARTRIDGES REMAIN. The orange magazine follower is visible in the feedthroat when the magazine is empty.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — How to Unload — p.6

steps.title: Close the action, then prove it once more before any screw turns
steps.action: With the safety on SAFE and the inner magazine tube locked, unload the gun and check again that no cartridges remain, then close the action completely. This is a second, deliberate check made at the start of the disassembly rather than at the end of shooting — Marlin repeats it because the rifle is about to come apart in your hands.
steps.quote:
Step #1 — With the safety on SAFE and the inner magazine tube locked in place, unload
the gun and visually check to be doubly sure no cartridges remain. Then close the action
completely.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the Action, Step #1 — p.7
steps.warn: Before cleaning your rifle, be certain it is completely unloaded, and the bolt has been removed.

steps.title: Safety glasses on before the action comes apart
steps.action: Put safety glasses on before you undo anything. There is a compressed recoil spring inside this receiver and the step that frees it is two moves away. Marlin asks for glasses specifically for the disassembly, not just for shooting.
steps.quote: 16. Wear impact-protective glasses when shooting, disassembling or cleaning firearms.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Safety rules, rule 16 — p.2

steps.title: Inner magazine tube out first
steps.action: Take the inner magazine tube out before the takedown screws, using the same motion as loading: unlock the knurled end plug and draw the inner tube out of the outer tube. Doing this first means the tube is not trapped when the barrelled action leaves the stock, and it lets you see straight down the empty tube one last time.
steps.quote:
Step #2 — The inner magazine tube should be removed in accordance with the
procedure described under “How to Load”.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the Action, Step #2 — p.8

steps.title: Both takedown screws out; rifle into two halves
steps.action: Unscrew takedown screws A and B and lift the rifle apart into two pieces: the stock with the trigger assembly in it, and the barrel with the action. They are not interchangeable screws in feel — one is the front and one the rear, so keep them apart on the bench so they go back where they came from.
steps.quote:
Step #3 — Unscrew takedown screws A and B as shown in K on page 7. Separate the
rifle into two segments, the first consisting of the stock and trigger assembly, the second
consisting of the barrel and action.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the Action, Step #3 — p.8

steps.title: Squeeze the assembly post and pull it free, then slide the action out
steps.action: Squeeze the slotted end of the assembly post and push it in — the slot lets it collapse enough to pass through its hole — then pull the post free of the action. With the post out, slide the action to the REAR and then up out of its channel. Rearward first, then up: try to lift it straight out and it will not clear.
steps.quote:
Release assembly post by squeezing and
pushing in slotted end.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the Action — p.8

steps.title: Charging handle back, lift the MUZZLE end of the bolt out
steps.action: This is the step that bites. Pull the charging handle back slightly and, with the forefinger of the other hand, lift the MUZZLE end of the breech bolt up out of the receiver — the front of the bolt, not the back. As the front comes up the charging handle goes slack and can be pulled straight out. Keep control of the bolt while you do it: the recoil spring is compressed behind it and can throw itself out of the receiver.
steps.prose: Lifting the rear of the bolt first jams it against the receiver rails and people then pull harder, which is how the bolt and the receiver both get marked.
steps.quote:
Pull the charging handle back slightly
and, with the forefinger of your other
hand, lift the muzzle end of the bolt from
the receiver (See N).
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the Action — p.8
steps.warn: Recoil spring is compressed at this point and, if not handled properly, can fly from the receiver.

steps.title: Recoil spring and spring guide out — field strip complete
steps.action: With the bolt and charging handle out, the recoil spring and its guide are loose and lift straight out of the receiver. That is the Model 60 stripped: stock, barrelled action, assembly post, breech bolt, charging handle, recoil spring and spring guide. Marlin stops here, and so should you — further disassembly of the action is not recommended and is a gunsmith's or the factory's job.
steps.quote: Further disassembly of the action is not recommended and should only be attempted by a qualified gunsmith or the factory.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the Action, Step #5 — p.8
steps.warn: Recoil spring is compressed at this point and, if not handled properly, can fly from the receiver.

steps.title: Bore, but only when it needs it
steps.action: Marlin's position on this rifle is that modern .22 ammunition burns clean enough that routine bore cleaning is not necessary. Clean the bore if the rifle got wet, or if anything foreign found its way into the action or barrel. Use a standard .22 rod and patches, powder solvent through it, then a light wipe of gun oil.
steps.quote:
To clean the bore and barrel, use any standard .22 caliber commercial cleaning rod
and cleaning patches. Clean the barrel with powder solvent and wipe lightly with gun
oil after cleaning.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the bore — p.7

steps.title: The 250-round interval: receiver, bolt face, extractors, chamber end
steps.action: The interval that actually matters on this rifle is the action, not the bore. Clean the inside of the receiver, the bolt face, both extractors and the breech end of the barrel around the chamber every 250 rounds or so, more often with dirtier ammunition. A toothbrush and gun solvent is the whole kit.
steps.prose: .22 rimfire is a filthy, waxy round and this is a blowback action — carbon and bullet lube pack into the bolt face and around the extractors, and that is what causes the failures to feed and eject people blame on the magazine.
steps.caution: Be sure to follow manufacturer of gun cleaner's directions, as some chemicals may damage the synthetic trigger guard.
steps.quote:
We recommend cleaning the inside of the
receiver, bolt face, extractors, and butt
end of the barrel (around the chamber)
after firing each 250 rounds.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the Action — p.7

steps.title: Action in solvent, dried, then oiled sparingly
steps.action: With the barrel, receiver and action out of the stock, clean the action in solvent, dry it, and oil it sparingly before it goes back together. Sparingly is the operative word on a rimfire: oil left standing in a blowback receiver mixes with the wax off the bullets and turns into a paste that stops the bolt short.
steps.quote:
The action
should be cleaned in solvent, dried,
and oiled sparingly prior to reassembly.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — Cleaning the Action — p.8

steps.title: Solvent check before it touches the finish
steps.action: Read the label of any solvent or cleaning product before it goes near this rifle and check it will not attack the finish or the parts. That is not boilerplate here — the trigger guard on these rifles is synthetic and some gun-cleaning chemicals will craze it. Test in an inconspicuous place if you are not sure.
steps.quote:
Caution: Before using any solvent or other gun cleaning product, read the label 
carefully to be sure it will not damage either the finish or any parts of this firearm.
steps.cite: SELF-LOADING Rifle (22 L.R. only) With Tubular Magazine — Owner's Manual — 20201222 (the date code in the published filename; no printed edition line) — How to Clean Your Rifle — p.7

deepAbsentReason: Marlin publishes no procedure beyond this strip for the Model 60. Its own words at the end of the disassembly sequence are that further disassembly of the action is not recommended and should only be attempted by a qualified gunsmith or the factory. The book's remaining pages are the parts list and warranty; there is no trigger-group, extractor or firing-pin teardown in it, and inventing one would be inventing a deep clean.

cleaning.name: Receiver and action
tasks: Every ~250 rounds: inside the receiver, the bolt face, the extractors and the breech end of the barrel around the chamber.
Toothbrush and commercial gun solvent; check the solvent will not attack the synthetic trigger guard.
Clean the action in solvent, dry it, oil it sparingly before reassembly.

cleaning.name: Bolt and springs
tasks: Bolt face and both extractor cuts scrubbed clear of wax and carbon.
Recoil spring and spring guide wiped clean — do not stretch the spring to 'restore' it.
Charging handle and its slot in the bolt wiped clean.

cleaning.name: Bore
tasks: Not routinely required on modern ammunition.
Clean if the rifle got wet or if foreign material entered the action or barrel.
Standard .22 rod and patches, powder solvent, light gun oil after.

cleaning.name: Exterior and storage
tasks: Wipe external metal with a lightly oiled cloth.
Stainless models: stainless can still rust — remove moisture and wipe down with oil or a rust inhibitor.
Below freezing: a very thin coat of light oil only, and remove all condensation afterwards.
Long-term storage: lightly oil bore, barrel and action; store unloaded in a dry area, never in a carrying case.

reassembly: Recoil spring guide into one end of the recoil spring; the other end of the spring into the breech bolt.
Recoil spring guide into the hole at the rear of the receiver.
Hold bolt and spring in one hand and support the spring with the other while compressing it, so the spring cannot kink.
Charging handle in through the ejection port and into its slot in the bolt.
Pull the charging handle fully back and lock the action open, then reverse the action removal to seat it.
Assembly post back through the action until it latches.
Barrelled action into the stock with the receiver seated as far REARWARD in the stock as it will go before the takedown screws are tightened — otherwise the rifle may not fire.
Inner magazine tube back into the outer tube and the knurled end plug rotated to the locked position.
fncheck: With the rifle proven empty and the muzzle safe: pull the charging handle fully rearward and confirm the action locks open, then release it and confirm the bolt runs fully home under spring pressure with no hesitation. Push the safety to SAFE and back to FIRE and confirm both positions are positive. Cycle the action several times by hand and listen for the bolt seating fully — a bolt that stops short means the receiver was not seated fully rearward in the stock when the takedown screws were tightened, and Marlin's own warning is that the rifle may then not fire. Check the bore is clear before loading.
